passage: Twelve minutes on the clock, eight candidates around one table, and a ceiling fan that drowned every third word. Kalyani's foot tapped under the table. Each time someone opened their mouth she heard a rival for the one seat, and she wanted to shout over the lot of them. She did it once, cutting off a boy mid-sentence, and saw the panellist's pen stop. Her ears went hot. Then Ritu, across the table, made a point about flexible hours that Kalyani had not thought of. Kalyani took a breath. "Building on Ritu's point," she said, "the cost side matters too," and she added two clear lines and stopped. The panellist's pen began to move again.

qa.q: How many minutes were on the clock?
qa.a: Twelve minutes were on the clock.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel about the other candidates at first?
qa.a: She felt tense and competitive, hearing each of them as a rival for the one seat and wanting to shout over the lot of them.

qa.q: What could Kalyani try in the next group discussion?
qa.a: She could give clear points, credit a good idea from someone else, and leave space for others to speak.

qa.q: How might the panellist have seen Kalyani's two moments?
qa.a: Cutting a boy off may look like someone who struggles to work with others, while building on Ritu's point shows someone who can; the pen stopped and then moved again.

grounding: In a group discussion Kalyani sees others as obstacles and shouts one down, then credits a good point and contributes clearly.

passage:
Sharmila: GD round tomorrow. 8 people, 1 topic, 15 min. I plan to talk the most 💪
Nikita: talk the most or say the best thing?
Sharmila: same thing. if I don't grab the floor someone else will
Nikita: our placement senior said panels mark people who interrupt as poor team players
Sharmila: ugh. so I just sit quietly?
Nikita: no. make 2-3 clear points. and when someone says something good, build on it and say their name
Sharmila: that feels like helping the competition
Nikita: it shows you can work with people. that's literally what they're hiring for
(next evening)
Sharmila: ok update. I didn't interrupt once
Sharmila: a boy made a smart point about rural internet and I said 'building on Faisal's point' and the moderator looked up and smiled 🙂
Nikita: and??
Sharmila: shortlisted for the interview!!

qa.q: How many people were in the GD?
qa.a: There were 8 people in the GD.

qa.q: What does 'if I don't grab the floor someone else will' suggest Sharmila was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Sharmila felt anxious and competitive, seeing the others as obstacles.
Making a few clear points and building on others' ideas by name showed the panel someone who can work with others.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Faisal to hear 'building on Faisal's point'?
qa.a: Faisal would likely feel respected and included rather than shouted down, which makes the discussion better for everyone.

grounding: A chat shows a candidate who sees GD rivals as obstacles learning to make clear points and credit others instead of talking over them.

passage: The group discussion for the cooperative bank trainee posts was held in a stuffy upstairs hall in Pala, a small town in Kottayam district. Thomas had decided on the bus: be loud, be first, be remembered. When Anjali began explaining how the self-help groups in her village ran their meetings, he cut in over her: 'That's just one example, the real issue is...' A panel member tapped a pen. Thomas saw it, and saw Anjali's face close. For a few minutes he kept talking, faster, but the room had gone cold. Then he stopped. 'Sorry. Anjali, finish your point about the self-help groups, it was strong.' She did, and it was. He added two facts from his project on crop loans, and a quieter boy by the window got a turn too. Afterwards, on the stairs, Anjali said, 'Thanks for handing it back.' Thomas said, 'I shouldn't have taken it.'

qa.q: Where was the group discussion held?
qa.a: It was held in a stuffy upstairs hall in Pala.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when the panel member tapped a pen?
qa.a: Thomas felt uneasy and under pressure, talking faster as he sensed the room turning cold.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Talking over Anjali went wrong; apologising, handing the floor back and crediting her point fixed it.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt when Thomas cut in?
qa.a: Anjali likely felt dismissed and shut out, as her face closed, and later appreciated him handing it back.

grounding: Shows a candidate treating a group discussion as a fight to be heard, noticing the cost, and switching to crediting others.
